An AI phone host like ROAL can answer the restaurant's phone, take pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It is built for busy restaurants, and it can be a useful fit for wing shops that want fewer missed calls and less back-and-forth.

sections.h2: What does a wings phone order need to capture?
sections.body:
A wing order sounds simple until the caller starts stacking details. Wings shops usually need the size, sauce, dry rub, heat level, sides, dips, and whether the order is for pickup or delivery. If the order is for a big game night, you may also need notes like extra napkins, no celery, or "separate sauces."

A phone host should ask for the same details every time. That keeps the kitchen from guessing. ROAL can take items, sizes, modifiers, and notes from the live menu, then confirm the order back before it sends the ticket.

Use a script like this:
- "Thanks for calling. What size wing order would you like today?"
- "What sauce or dry rub should I put on that?"
- "Any sides, dips, or special notes?"

For a wing shop, the order should be complete enough that the cook can read it once and start cooking.

sections.h2: How do wing shops handle flavors, sauces, and add-ons by phone?
sections.body:
Wing menus can get messy fast. Some guests order 10 wings split between two sauces. Others want boneless, extra wet, mild plus garlic parmesan, or a combo with fries. The phone host has to keep up without losing the thread.

The cleanest setup is to think in menu steps. First size. Then style. Then flavor. Then add-ons. For example, the host might say: "I have 20 bone-in wings. Which sauce would you like on them?" If the caller wants split sauces, the host should ask how many in each flavor and repeat it back.

Here is a practical checklist for wing menus:
- Sizes: 6, 10, 20, or your own sizes
- Style: bone-in or boneless
- Sauce or dry rub: one or split
- Heat level: mild, medium, hot, or your own labels
- Add-ons: fries, celery, ranch, blue cheese, extra sauce

ROAL reads the live menu, so sold-out items should not be offered. That helps avoid a painful call where the caller wants a flavor you cannot make.

sections.h2: How do you keep rush-hour calls from slowing the kitchen?
sections.body:
Wing shops often feel the pressure when games start, rain hits, or the dinner rush stacks up. That is when the phone rings the most. If the staff is frying, boxing, or bagging, the phone can turn into a line of its own.

A good phone flow should cut time without cutting clarity. ROAL can answer the call, take the order, quote a ready time, confirm the order back, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. If the question is something the host cannot answer, it goes to the inbox and staff can answer it once so the host learns it for next time.

A simple rush checklist for wing shops:
1. Make sure the live menu is current.
2. Confirm hours and pickup rules are correct.
3. Set the ready-time language your staff uses.
4. Decide which calls should forward only when busy or unanswered.
5. Test-call the host before a big game or weekend rush.

sections.h2: What should you say on the phone so the order is clear?
sections.body:
Wing calls go smoother when the wording is short and repeatable. You do not need fancy language. You need a clear path from hello to ticket.

A practical phone script for a wing shop can sound like this:
"Thanks for calling. What can I get started for you?"
"Is that pickup or delivery?"
"How many wings would you like, and what flavor?"
"Any fries, dips, or notes?"
"Your order will be ready in about 25 minutes. Can I get your name and phone number?"

That script works because it moves in the same order the kitchen needs. It also catches the basics: item, size, flavor, notes, name, phone, and ready time.

Here is a short order template you can use with staff or compare against your own setup:

| Order detail | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Item | 20 bone-in wings |
| Sauce | Half hot, half garlic parmesan |
| Add-ons | Large fries, 2 ranches |
| Name | Maria |
| Phone | Caller number |
| Ready time | 25 minutes |

ROAL can speak the caller's language and confirm the full order back before sending the ticket.

sections.h2: How do you set up call forwarding without losing control?
sections.body:
Many wing shops already have a number customers know. You do not need to give that up. With ROAL, the owner claims the host, gets a phone line for each location, and forwards the restaurant's existing number to it. Forward all calls, or only when busy or unanswered. The restaurant keeps its own number, and forwarding can be turned off any time.

If you are setting up forwarding yourself, carrier codes vary. On many landlines and some carriers, *72 forwards all calls and *73 turns it off. On some GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually set this in the web portal. Always confirm with your carrier and test with a call.

Use this setup checklist:
- Confirm your forwarding choice: all calls, busy only, or unanswered only
- Test a real call from a mobile phone
- Check that the host answers with the right restaurant name
- Make sure the kitchen gets the ticket
- Turn forwarding off when you want to change the setup

faq.q: Can an AI phone host take a wings phone order with split sauces?
faq.a: Yes. It can ask how many wings go to each sauce, confirm the split back to the caller, and send the details to the kitchen screen. That is important for wing shops because split flavors are common and easy to mishear.

faq.q: Will the phone host tell callers about sold-out wing flavors?
faq.a: It should not offer items marked sold out. ROAL reads the live menu, so if you remove a flavor or item, it will stop offering it on the phone. That helps prevent awkward orders the kitchen cannot fill.

faq.q: Can it handle allergy questions or manager requests?
faq.a: Yes, but those calls go to staff with a summary. ROAL can handle allergy-sensitive questions, catering, complaints, and manager requests by handing them off instead of guessing. That keeps the conversation safer and cleaner.

faq.q: How do I forward my wing shop number to the host?
faq.a: You can forward your existing number to ROAL after claiming the host. Many carriers use codes like *72 or carrier-specific mobile forwarding codes, but the exact steps depend on your phone system and plan. Always confirm with your carrier and test with a real call.
